explanations.explanation: Flint it is, baker. The LORD tells Joshua, “Make flint knives and circumcise the sons of Israel once again.” Then Joshua makes them (Joshua 5:2-3). I'm a cookie stamper, so my whole toolbox is one handle with my name carved in it. Knife making is way above my pay grade.
Bronze sounds fancy, friend, like something you'd put on a trophy shelf. But the LORD says, “Make flint knives…” Flint, not bronze. Joshua follows that word and makes them.

Iron sounds sturdy, and I respect that. Once upon a time I got swapped out for a shinier stamper, so I know all about upgrades. But the LORD tells Joshua, “Make flint knives…” Flint is the word, and Joshua makes them.

explanations.answer: None of them had been circumcised
explanations.explanation: None. Not one. The text says it plainly: “…none of those born in the wilderness on the journey from Egypt had been circumcised.” The ones who came out of Egypt were circumcised, but their sons born along the way were not (Joshua 5:5). That's a whole generation waiting on Joshua's flint knives.

explanations.answer: Only the firstborn had been circumcised
explanations.explanation: That sounds neat and tidy, but the text doesn't mention firstborn sons at all. It says none of those born in the wilderness on the journey had been circumcised. Not just the later ones, not just the younger ones. None, and that's why Joshua has work to do.

explanations.answer: Most had been circumcised on the way
explanations.explanation: I get the guess, friend. You'd think somebody would have taken care of it somewhere in forty years. But Joshua 5:7 says it straight: they had not been circumcised along the way. It wasn't most. The text says none of them had been.

explanations.answer: They did not obey the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives: “…since they did not obey the LORD.” So the LORD vowed never to let them see the land He had sworn to their fathers (Joshua 5:6). The wandering went on until those men of war had died. No guessing needed here, because the verse tells us why.

explanations.answer: They were struck down by Egypt's army
explanations.explanation: Egypt's army doesn't show up anywhere in this passage, friend. The text says these men died in the wilderness, and it gives one reason: they did not obey the LORD. They had already left Egypt behind (Joshua 5:4). The reason is right there in verse 6.

explanations.answer: They ran out of food on the journey
explanations.explanation: I see why that one tempts you, since a long trip makes you think about snacks. But the text gives a different reason: they did not obey the LORD. Food isn't named as the cause of anything here. In fact, the manna kept coming until the very end of this passage (Joshua 5:12).

I know it's a tough thing to hear, baker, but the text says the opposite. The LORD vowed never to let those men see the land He had sworn to their fathers to give. That land is “…a land flowing with milk and honey.” (Joshua 5:6). So the answer is False, because that was the vow.

False is right. Joshua 5:6 says the LORD “…vowed never to let them see the land He had sworn to their fathers to give us…” It's the land flowing with milk and honey, and that generation of men of war died without seeing it. I think that's a heavy one, so I'll just say it once and let it sit.

Healed, yes. Joshua 5:8 says that after the whole nation had been circumcised, they stayed there in the camp until they were healed. They stayed put. I know a little about staying put, since I once spent years in the back of a junk drawer. Nobody was healing me back there, I was just collecting dust.
Counting sounds like a very organized thing to do, and I like organized. But the text doesn't mention a count here. It says they stayed there in the camp until they were healed (Joshua 5:8).

Anointed is a good-sounding word, friend, but it's not the one in this verse. After the whole nation had been circumcised, they stayed in the camp until they were healed. That's what Joshua 5:8 says. Healing came first, and everybody stayed right there.

Gilgal, baker. After the LORD says, “Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you.” the verse tells us, “So that place has been called Gilgal to this day.” (Joshua 5:9). That "…to this day." means the name was still in use when the writer wrote it. It's the same camp the Israelites are in when they keep the Passover (Joshua 5:10).

Bethel isn't the name this verse gives. Joshua 5:9 says, “So that place has been called Gilgal to this day.” The camp on the plains of Jericho is where the LORD speaks, and that's the place that gets the name. It's an easy one to second-guess, friend.

Shiloh isn't the name in this verse. After the LORD rolls away the reproach of Egypt, the text says, “So that place has been called Gilgal to this day.” Gilgal is where Israel is camped (Joshua 5:10). Easy one to mix up, so no worries.

Passover is right. Joshua 5:10 says that on the evening of the fourteenth day of the month, while camped at Gilgal on the plains of Jericho, the Israelites kept it. Before that, the LORD had said, “Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you.” (Joshua 5:9). Keep that evening in mind, baker.

The Sabbath is a good guess, friend, but the text names something else for that fourteenth evening. Joshua 5:10 says the Israelites kept the Passover. The Sabbath doesn't come up in this passage, so the fourteenth day is your clue.

Purim is a fair guess, baker, but it isn't the one in this verse. The text says that on the evening of the fourteenth day, the Israelites kept the Passover (Joshua 5:10). They kept it while camped at Gilgal on the plains of Jericho. Purim doesn't come up in this passage.

explanations.answer: Unleavened bread and roasted grain from the land
explanations.explanation: Unleavened bread and roasted grain, and it all came from the produce of the land. Joshua 5:11 says they ate it the day after the Passover, on that very day. I'm a cookie guy, so I went looking for chocolate chips in that verse and came up empty. Bread and roasted grain from the land is what the text gives.

explanations.answer: Fish they caught in the Jordan River
explanations.explanation: Fish would make a fine dinner, friend, but this verse doesn't mention any. The Israelites ate unleavened bread and roasted grain from the produce of the land. That's what Joshua 5:11 says. The Jordan River doesn't come up here at all.

explanations.answer: Grain they had bought from the people of Jericho
explanations.explanation: That's a creative idea, baker, but the text doesn't say anything about buying. Joshua 5:11 says they ate unleavened bread and roasted grain “…from the produce of the land.” The verse puts the food in the land itself. No shopping trip is mentioned.

The manna stopped. Joshua 5:12 says, “…the manna ceased. There was no more manna for the Israelites…” That year they began to eat the crops of the land of Canaan. Nobody said anything about missing it, so I'll just say the cookies in my bakery never come with a stop date.

The quail is a good thought, but this verse doesn't name them. What stopped is the manna. Joshua 5:12 says, “There was no more manna for the Israelites…” After that, they ate the crops of the land of Canaan.

The cloud isn't in this passage, friend. What the text says ceased is the manna. “There was no more manna for the Israelites, so that year they began to eat the crops of the land of Canaan.” (Joshua 5:12). That's the change the verse records.
